cases.event: Over many years, lightning struck the hilltop at the fictional park {E} far more often than the land around it.
cases.q: What most likely caused lightning to strike the hilltop at {E} so often?
restate: Lightning struck the hilltop at {E} unusually often, and the question asks why.
Something made the hilltop at {E} a frequent target for lightning.
cases.answer: The hilltop's height most likely caused it to be struck so often, because lightning tends to strike the tallest point in an area.
cases.sum: the evidence points to the hilltop's height as the reason it was struck so often.
cases.myth: The hilltop at {E} was struck often because lightning enjoys the view from high places.
cases.mythClause: lightning struck only on days with a full moon
cases.altText: Some visitors suggested that iron in the hilltop's rocks was drawing lightning to {E}.
cases.patternQ: What pattern connects height and lightning strikes at {E}?
cases.patternA: The hilltop was struck often while it was the tallest point and rarely after a taller tower was built nearby, so the strikes followed the height.
cases.patternSum: the hilltop was struck often only while it was the tallest point.

prediction.text: Years ago, a visitor predicted that the radio mast in the valley below {E} would rarely be struck because it stands on low ground.
prediction.claim: the radio mast in the valley below {E} would rarely be struck
prediction.whyNot: the tall radio mast in the valley was struck almost as often as the hilltop

cases.observerNote: The rangers recorded every lightning strike they saw.

obs.text: Over {n0} years, the hilltop at {E} was struck about twice a year, while the fields below were rarely struck.
exps: the hilltop was struck again and again while the lower fields were not, which points to its height
the difference between the hilltop and the low fields fits height as the cause
being high above the fields made the hilltop a frequent target

obs.text: The hilltop at {E} rises about {n1} meters above the valley and is the highest point for many kilometers.
exps: lightning tends to strike the tallest object around, and the hilltop is the tallest point for kilometers
this shows why the hilltop was a target, since its height gives lightning the shortest path to the ground
being the highest point explains how the hilltop drew so many strikes

obs.text: After a taller tower with a lightning rod was built on a nearby hill, strikes on the hilltop at {E} became rare.
obs.tag: the strikes after the tower was built
exps: once the hilltop was no longer the tallest point, it stopped being struck often, which is what height would predict
the strikes moved to the taller tower, so height and strikes are linked
once the cause changed, the effect changed with it

obs.text: Rock samples showed that the hilltop at {E} contains no more iron than the rocks in the valley.
exps: if the hilltop has no extra iron, iron cannot explain why it was struck more often
this rules out iron, because the rocks were the same as in the valley
with no extra iron present, the iron explanation has nothing to stand on

obs.text: A tall radio mast in the valley below {E} was struck almost as often as the hilltop.
exps: the mast stands on ordinary valley rock, yet it was struck often because it is tall
this rules out iron, since a tall object without iron-rich rock was struck just as much
height, not the rock beneath, is what the mast and the hilltop have in common
predExps: this directly contradicts the prediction, since the mast was struck almost as often as the hilltop
if low ground protected the mast, it would rarely be struck, but it was struck often
the prediction expected few strikes on the mast, and the observations show many
